And the smallest meaningful program is a LightningModule plus a Trainer, straight from the repository’s quick start:

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.utils.data as data, torchvision as tv
import torch.nn.functional as F
import lightning as L

class LitAutoEncoder(L.LightningModule):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(28 * 28, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 3))
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 28 * 28))

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.encoder(x)

    def training_step(self, batch, batch_idx):
        x, _ = batch
        x = x.view(x.size(0), -1)
        z = self.encoder(x)
        x_hat = self.decoder(z)
        loss = F.mse_loss(x_hat, x)
        self.log("train_loss", loss)
        return loss

    def configure_optimizers(self):
        return torch.optim.Adam(self.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

dataset = tv.datasets.MNIST(".", download=True, transform=tv.transforms.ToTensor())
train, val = data.random_split(dataset, [55000, 5000])

autoencoder = LitAutoEncoder()
trainer = L.Trainer()
trainer.fit(autoencoder, data.DataLoader(train), data.DataLoader(val))

That program runs unchanged on a GPU box with the DDP strategy enabled, accumulates gradients with a flag, resumes from a checkpoint with another, and swaps optimizers’ precision with a third. The science stayed in the class; the engineering moved into the framework.

Honest limits: the abstraction has real weight. Debugging a training bug means learning where your code ends and the loop engine begins, and the hook ordering has enough surface area that newcomers occasionally fight the framework instead of the bug. The rename from pytorch-lightning to lightning left two import namespaces and a long deprecation trail. Expert users who want tight control often graduate to Fabric, which is both a feature and an admission that the Trainer is not for everyone. And the loop engine, restartable as it is, still assumes batch-centric training; genuinely exotic schedules end up in manual optimization mode anyway. None of this dims the core achievement: this repository turned the world’s most repeated training boilerplate into a maintained, tested, hardware-portable foundation, which is why so much modern AI code starts with import lightning.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Lightning-AI/pytorch-lightning: how the Trainer facade, the LightningModule contract, the loop engine, and a Strategy family from DDP to DeepSpeed turn raw PyTorch into scalable training, with Fabric as the expert escape hatch.

entry.title: One Framework, Four Kinds of Retrieval - Inside UKPLab/sentence-transformers

link.title: One Framework, Four Kinds of Retrieval - Inside UKPLab/sentence-transformers

entry.content:
In 2019, two researchers at the UKP Lab in TU Darmstadt published Sentence-BERT and open-sourced the code that made transformer embeddings practical for sentences. Six years later that codebase, UKPLab/sentence-transformers under the Apache-2.0 license and now maintained within Hugging Face, has grown into the framework behind more than fifteen thousand pretrained models on the Hub and a permanent fixture of the MTEB retrieval leaderboard. The current development line, version 6.2.0, is no longer just sentence embeddings: the same package now ships four model families, SentenceTransformer for dense embeddings, CrossEncoder for reranking, SparseEncoder for SPLADE-style sparse vectors, and MultiVectorEncoder for ColBERT-style late interaction, all behind one import and one training story. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The architecture earns its simplicity through a shared core. Every family inherits from a single BaseModel that is literally an nn.Sequential of modules: a Transformer input module loads any Hugging Face checkpoint, then pooling, projection, and normalization modules shape the output. Each family is a thin subclass that adds its own encode-style methods, its own trainer glue, and its own loss library, while saving, hub uploads, multimodal inputs, batching, and backend exports live once in the base. Reading the overview from left to right follows that story: four facades, one core, one training bridge, and a utility belt from similarity math to ONNX export.

Overview of sentence-transformers: four family facades extend one BaseModel core built from composable modules, the BaseTrainer bridges Hugging Face's Trainer, and utilities plus export backends round out the package.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • SentenceTransformer is the flagship at line 38 of 1341 lines, with encode implemented at 753 and the similarity method at 1056.
  • CrossEncoder is the reranker at line 32 of 826 lines: predict at 450 scores text pairs, rank at 642 returns ordered passages.
  • SparseEncoder at line 30 of 1473 lines produces vocabulary-sized sparse vectors, with a static sparsity reporter at 1157.
  • MultiVectorEncoder at line 63 of 1623 lines emits one vector per token, scored by MaxSim at 977.
  • BaseModel is the shared core at line 66 of 2045 lines, with save_pretrained at 806 and push_to_hub at 950.
  • The Transformer module is the input module at line 644 that wraps any Hugging Face checkpoint, dispatching by Router at line 30 for non-text modalities.
  • BaseTrainer is the training bridge at line 89 of 1334 lines, extending the Hugging Face Trainer for all four families.
  • util/similarity.py is the math belt of 940 lines: cos_sim at 59, dot_score at 101, manhattan at 135, each with pairwise variants.

Why You Need This

Retrieval is not one algorithm, it is a menu of trade-offs, and this repository is the only mainstream library that puts the whole menu behind one API. Dense embeddings compress a sentence into one vector: fast to search, occasionally lossy. A CrossEncoder reads query and passage together and scores them jointly: accurate, too slow to run over a whole corpus, which is exactly why it exists as a reranker. Sparse vectors keep the vocabulary dimension, so matching is transparent and lexical. Late interaction keeps one vector per token and scores with MaxSim, trading storage for fine-grained matching. Learning all four from scratch means four codebases; here they are four classes with the same load, save, encode, and similarity conventions.

The second reason is the module system, which is genuinely compositional rather than nominally so. A model is a chain: put a Transformer at the front, append Pooling to turn tokens into one vector, optionally a Dense projection or Normalize at the end, save it, and the chain definition travels with the weights. Swap Pooling for a sparse pooling module and the same skeleton produces SPLADE vectors; swap the front for StaticEmbedding lookup tables and you get CPU-friendly models that the project blogs about running dramatically faster than attention-based ones. Because every module implements the same save and load contract at the Module base class, custom research modules slot into pretrained models without forks.

The third reason is the training story, which is where most embedding projects stall. The library ships roughly twenty-eight embedding loss functions, from MultipleNegativesRankingLoss to cached variants that grow batch sizes to thousands of negatives, plus a dozen reranker losses and a dozen sparse losses, all feeding one Hugging Face Trainer subclass so you get mixed precision, multi-GPU, and logging for free. Evaluation runs during training with eleven ready evaluators, hard negatives can be mined from any corpus with one function call, and trained models auto-generate full model cards for the Hub. That is a complete path from raw pairs to a searchable, shareable artifact.

The detailed map: family facades and their key methods, the BaseModel core with save, hub, cards, adapters, and modality handling, the module stack, the training bridge with losses and samplers, evaluators, and the utility and backend layer.

The cleanest place to understand this codebase is the inheritance diamond that is not. BaseModel at line 66 declares itself as nn.Sequential, PeftAdapterMixin, and ABC, which means a model instance is simultaneously the module chain, a loadable adapter host, and a family contract. Its 2045 lines carry the universal verbs: save_pretrained at 806 walks the module chain and serializes each module’s config and state, push_to_hub at 950 packages the folder with the model card machinery from a 2052-line model_card.py, and the 941-line modality.py defines how text, image, audio, and video inputs are named, processed, and routed. The Router at line 30 picks the right input module per modality, which is how the CLIP module and the text Transformer coexist in one framework.

The family facades then differentiate on output shape. SentenceTransformer’s encode at 753 is the single-vector path, with encode_multi_process at 1101 for corpus-scale jobs and similarity at 1056 dispatching to cosine, dot, euclidean, or manhattan. CrossEncoder’s predict at 450 feeds pairs through the transformer and a scoring head, and rank at 642 wraps predict with sorting so the README’s three-passage Berlin query returns corpus ids, scores, and texts in order, with the ms-marco MiniLM checkpoint printing 8.61, 6.35, and 5.51 for its three candidates. SparseEncoder’s encode at 578 produces a vector the width of the vocabulary, and its static sparsity method at 1157 reports what the README demonstrates on a SPLADE model: ninety-nine point eight percent of activations are zero. MultiVectorEncoder splits into encode_query at 355 and encode_document at 531, then scores with MaxSim at 977, where each query token picks its best-matching document token, which is why the README example encodes a ten-token query into a 10 by 128 matrix and scores a Paris document at 9.60 against a Berlin one at 9.41.

Training is deliberately boring in the best way. SentenceTransformerTrainer is only 168 lines at line 36 because the 1334-line BaseTrainer at line 89 already extends the Hugging Face Trainer with column remapping, multi-dataset sampling through an 806-line sampler, and a 187-line collator that pairs texts with labels. The loss libraries are where the research lives: the CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss at line 26 is one of twenty-eight embedding losses, caching gradient-safe negatives so contrastive training scales without OOM. The legacy fit method survives at line 160 of fit_mixin.py as a compatibility path that compiles old-style arguments into the trainer stack.

The last mile is deployment and data, and both get real code rather than afterthoughts. mine_hard_negatives at line 25 of a 948-line module scans a corpus with an existing model to manufacture difficult negatives, the single highest-leverage trick for embedding quality. quantization.py compresses embeddings to binary and scalar forms across 564 lines for cheaper indexes. And the backend layer loads ONNX models at line 14 and OpenVINO at 92, with export helpers for optimized ONNX at optimize.py line 19, dynamic ONNX quantization at quantize.py line 24, and static OpenVINO quantization at line 109, so a trained model leaves Python behind without leaving the framework.

From Install to Embeddings

The stack asks for Python 3.10 or newer, PyTorch 2.2 or newer, and transformers v5 or newer:

pip install -U sentence-transformers

Then the canonical example from the repository’s README:

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

sentences = [
    "The weather is lovely today.",
    "It's so sunny outside!",
    "He drove to the stadium.",
]
embeddings = model.encode(sentences)
print(embeddings.shape)
# => (3, 384)

similarities = model.similarity(embeddings, embeddings)
print(similarities)
# tensor([[1.0000, 0.6660, 0.1046],
#         [0.6660, 1.0000, 0.1411],
#         [0.1046, 0.1411, 1.0000]])

Three sentences become three 384-dimensional vectors, and one matrix multiplication answers which sentences mean the same thing. Swap the class name for CrossEncoder, SparseEncoder, or MultiVectorEncoder and the same four-line shape serves reranking, sparse search, or late interaction, with the repo even shipping an agent skill, installable via hf skills add train-sentence-transformers, that lets coding agents drive the training APIs directly.

Honest limits: the four-family breadth is new, and the seams show in version churn, with the jump to Trainer-based training in v3 and the multimodal expansion still leaving deprecation trails that the codebase keeps politely shimming. The legacy fit path exists precisely because a decade of tutorials depends on it. Rerankers and late-interaction models are compute-hungry at query time, and the library will not make a CrossEncoder cheap, only easy. Sparse and multi-vector support, while first-class, leans on a smaller model zoo than the dense family. And the module-chain design, elegant as it is, means a model directory is a contract: load a chain you did not build and you inherit its preprocessing decisions. Still, the core achievement stands: one import gives you four decades-worth of retrieval research in a shape you can actually ship, which is why sentence-transformers remains the default answer to how do I embed text.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of UKPLab/sentence-transformers: how SentenceTransformer, CrossEncoder, SparseEncoder, and MultiVectorEncoder share one BaseModel of composable modules, one HF Trainer bridge, and one set of similarity utilities to serve dense, reranked, sparse, and late-interaction retrieval.

entry.title: Post-Training, the PyTorch Way - Inside pytorch/torchtune

link.title: Post-Training, the PyTorch Way - Inside pytorch/torchtune

entry.content:
Fine-tuning an LLM used to mean choosing between a framework that hid PyTorch from you and a notebook that hid correctness from you. Torchtune, released by Meta’s PyTorch team in April 2024 under the BSD 3-Clause license, took a third path: native PyTorch recipes you can read in an afternoon, designed to be copied and edited rather than configured into submission. In roughly a year and a half, its 150-plus contributors shipped every major post-training method, from supervised finetuning through knowledge distillation, DPO, PPO, GRPO, and quantization-aware training, alongside from-scratch implementations of twenty model families including Llama4, Gemma2, Phi4, and Qwen3, and the memory numbers it published became the industry’s reference points: an 8B model fully finetuned on a single 4090 at 18.9 GiB, or QLoRA’d at 7.4 GiB. Development wound down in 2025, which makes the repository something better than a tool now: a completed, citable textbook. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The architecture is three flat layers with no framework between them. At the top, standalone recipe scripts in recipes/ are honest Python programs, each with a setup method that builds its objects and a train loop you can read line by line; YAML configs feed them through a thin OmegaConf layer, and the tune CLI with its five subcommands launches everything through torchrun. In the middle sits the torchtune package: a from-scratch transformer built on nn.Modules, an adapter shelf, a dataset layer, and the loss functions each method needs. At the bottom, a utilities shelf handles checkpointing across three checkpoint formats, FSDP2 wrapping, activation memory tricks, metric logging, and inference generation. Nothing is a plugin, nothing is registered in a registry, and every override happens through config dictionaries that map one-to-one onto function arguments. Reading the overview from left to right follows a YAML file all the way to GPU memory.

Overview of torchtune: the tune CLI loads YAML configs that instantiate recipes, recipes compose the TransformerDecoder core with LoRA adapters, the model zoo and dataset builders supply the objects, and training infrastructure handles checkpointing, distribution, and losses.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • TransformerDecoder at line 331 of 689 lines is the core, with self-attention layers at 17 and cross-attention at 144.
  • MultiHeadAttention at line 18 of 303 lines handles GQA, kv caching, and masks.
  • LoRALinear at line 27 of 320 lines is the adapter contract, with QATLoRALinear at 150.
  • The full finetune recipe is 718 lines: class at 39, setup at 235, train loop at 571.
  • The distributed recipe spans 1169 lines with FSDP2 sharding and multinode support.
  • The checkpointers cover 1478 lines in four formats: TorchTune at 122, HF at 369, Meta at 1039, Distributed at 1305.
  • DPOLoss at 181 lines implements the preference objective over policy and reference logprobs.
  • Llama3 builders in 240 lines wire 8B and 70B variants, with component builders at 510 lines.

Why You Need This

The first reason is that the recipes are the best documentation of post-training that exists in executable form. The single-device full finetune recipe is 718 lines including comments, and its train loop at line 571 shows exactly one epoch’s worth of decisions: gradient accumulation, clipping, activation checkpointing toggles, loss chunking, and checkpoint cadence, each guarded by a config field you can trace from the YAML. When the README tabulates how packed datasets raise throughput 238 percent or how activation checkpointing cuts active memory 42 percent, those numbers are produced by code paths you can walk in this repository, not by a benchmark harness you must take on faith. If you have ever wondered what your training framework actually does between your loss and your optimizer step, this is the rare place where the answer is not a cgo file or a registered plugin but a for loop you can annotate.

The second reason is the memory engineering, which treats every GiB as a budget line. The module shelf implements the full ladder from the README’s own table: sequence packing in the datasets layer, torch compile integration, chunked cross entropy that avoids materializing logits for the whole sequence, activation checkpointing and CPU offloading helpers, optimizer state fused into backward, 8-bit AdamW via bitsandbytes, and then the adapter ladder, LoRA at 8.5 GiB and QLoRA at 4.6 GiB for the same 3B model. The components are individually swappable, and the recipes compose them in the order the table recommends. For anyone deploying finetuning on constrained hardware, the value is not just the numbers but the fact that each technique is isolated in a file you can lift into your own trainer.

The third reason is interoperability as a first-class feature. The checkpointing layer speaks three dialects natively: torchtune’s own format, Hugging Face transformers, and Meta’s consolidated format, so a model you finetune here can be served by vLLM or the HF ecosystem without conversion scripts. Dataset builders consume Hugging Face datasets directly, evaluation runs through EleutherAI’s LM Eval Harness in a recipe, quantization goes through torchao, distributed training uses FSDP2, and the experimental GRPO stack integrates vLLM as a rollout engine with worker processes for weight syncing. The library treats the ecosystem as its user interface, which is a design lesson worth stealing even if you never finetune anything.

The detailed map: recipe scripts and config plumbing, the transformer module stack, the model zoo, dataset builders, training infrastructure, and the RLHF stack with its experimental workers.

Start where every run starts: the CLI and config. tune.py wires five subcommands in 56 lines, and run.py hands the YAML to the config layer, where _parse.py at 101 lines merges the recipe’s default config with your overrides, _validate.py checks required fields, and _instantiate.py turns dotted class paths like torchtune.models.llama3.llama3_8b into live objects with the remaining fields as keyword arguments. That is the entire magic: a config value loss=torchtune.modules.loss.CEWithChunkedOutputLoss becomes a Python object because one function splits the string and imports it. The recipes then read like scripts, and the flagship full finetune recipe at 718 lines builds model, tokenizer, optimizer, loss, and dataloader in setup at line 235, runs _loss_step at 551 which chunks the cross entropy and masks labels, and saves through the checkpointer at epoch and step boundaries; its distributed sibling at 1169 lines adds FSDP2 wrapping and multinode flags, and the LoRA variant at 753 lines swaps the model builder for lora_llama3_8b and checkpoints adapter state only.

The module layer is small enough to memorize and complete enough to trust. TransformerDecoder at line 331 assembles token embeddings, rotary positions from the 258-line position_embeddings module, scaling layers, and the self-attention layer at line 17, with a cross-attention sibling at 144 for vision-to-text models; MultiHeadAttention at 303 lines implements grouped query attention and feeds the 116-line KVCache during decode, and FeedForward at 54 lines plus rms_norm at 60 lines round out the block. The adapter shelf starts with LoRALinear at line 27, an AdapterModule whose A and B matrices carry all learning while the base weight freezes, extended by QATLoRALinear at 150 for fake-quantized training, a 206-line DoRA variant, and the 70-line NF4 linear for QLoRA’s 4-bit dtype. The loss shelf holds chunked cross entropy at 102 lines, the 440-line KD losses for distillation, and the preference losses that power the RLHF stack.

The model and data layers show what standardization buys. Twenty model family directories, from llama3 with its 240 lines of builders to llama4’s mixture-of-experts Scout, all construct the same TransformerDecoder with different component builders, which is why a new model lands as one directory of builders plus one config folder. The dataset layer’s fourteen builders, led by _instruct.py at 155 lines, share message transforms and tokenization so that instruct, chat, and preference data all produce the same dict of tensors; _packed.py implements the packed-batch strategy behind the README’s biggest throughput number, and _preference.py builds the chosen-and-rejected pairs that DPO consumes. Training infrastructure completes the picture: _checkpointer.py dedicates 1478 lines to the four format classes so weights move in and out of HF and Meta formats losslessly, _distributed.py’s 902 lines wrap FSDP2, memory.py’s 321 lines centralize the activation tricks, metric_logging.py’s 647 lines put disk, Weights and Biases, and Comet behind one interface, and generation’s 443-line inference loop with kv cache closes the loop for eval and rollout.

The RLHF stack is where recipes compose the hardest, and it rewards reading twice. The four DPO recipe variants drive DPOLoss at 181 lines, which needs both the policy and a frozen reference model’s logprobs over chosen and rejected sequences; PPO at 1246 recipe lines runs a full finetune with a value head and a reward model, using the 122-line PPOLoss and the reward helpers at 238 lines; and the dev/ directory carries the newest experiments, a GRPO implementation with its own generation and gsm8k task modules, plus an RL worker stack where vLLM serves as a parameter server, datacollectors assemble trajectories, and weight updaters sync parameters between training and rollout processes. QAT recipes tie back into the adapter shelf through QATLoRALinear, so even quantization-aware training follows the same recipe skeleton, and the quantize.py script plus eleuther_eval recipe finish the lifecycle after training.

From Install to a Finetune

The library tracks the latest stable PyTorch, currently 2.6.0, and leans on torchvision and torchao:

pip install torch torchvision torchao
pip install torchtune
tune --help

Download a gated model with your HF token, then finetune it with LoRA on one GPU:

tune download meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --output-dir /tmp/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --ignore-patterns "original/consolidated.00.pth" \
  --hf-token <HF_TOKEN>

tune run lora_finetune_single_device --config llama3_1/8B_lora_single_device

Two GPUs is one flag away, since the CLI fronts torchrun:

tune run --nproc_per_node 2 full_finetune_distributed --config llama3_1/8B_full

Everything is overridable from the command line, so batch_size=8, enable_activation_checkpointing=True, or max_steps_per_epoch=128 append directly to the command, and tune cp copies any config locally for heavier edits. To try the memory ladder yourself, run the QLoRA config with packed datasets and compile enabled, then watch peak memory fall to a few GiB while throughput climbs toward the README’s 284 percent number.

Honest limits: the project is no longer actively maintained, so treat it as a reference implementation rather than a dependency you expect updates from, and its tests target specific PyTorch versions. The recipes favor clarity over peak throughput, so production teams will leave some performance on the table compared to bespoke trainers. The model zoo, while broad, is text and vision only, and the experimental RL stack in dev/ is explicitly subject to change. And the CLI’s config-override power means a typo can silently train the wrong model, so validate configs before long runs. Read a recipe top to bottom, then the transformer, then the checkpointer; that order teaches you both the library and the anatomy of LLM finetuning itself.

entry.title: FP8 Without Rewriting Your Stack - Inside NVIDIA/TransformerEngine

link.title: FP8 Without Rewriting Your Stack - Inside NVIDIA/TransformerEngine

entry.content:
Training large models in FP8 promises roughly double the throughput and half the memory traffic of BF16, and the 2022 paper FP8 Formats for Deep Learning is the reason the industry believes it. The catch has always been numerics: eight-bit formats have tiny dynamic ranges, so every matmul needs scale factors, running maximums, and careful bookkeeping, and hand-rolling that across a transformer is a research project of its own. NVIDIA/TransformerEngine, the Apache-2.0 library behind FP8 training in Megatron-LM, NeMo, Hugging Face Accelerate, Lightning, and Amazon SageMaker, is the industrial answer: version 2.19, released in September 2026, carries FP8 recipes for Hopper through Rubin silicon plus MXFP8 and NVFP4 block scaling for Blackwell, fused kernels for attention, GEMMs, norms, and MoE, and a two-line API that hides all of it. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The repository splits into four packages: common holds the recipe definitions shared by every framework, pytorch is the 137-file flagship, jax mirrors the API across fifty files, and debug is a twenty-one-file numerics debugger. The design principle is separation of policy from mechanism. Recipes in common declare what precision policy you want; an autocast context manager in pytorch/quantization.py applies it region by region; a family of quantized tensor types carries the actual scaled data through the graph; and fused modules, from a plain Linear to a full TransformerLayer, call kernels that consume that data natively. Reading the overview from left to right traces one forward pass from recipe selection to quantized math to distributed infrastructure.

Overview of TransformerEngine: a shared recipe family feeds fp8_autocast, which quantizes work through fused modules into a QuantizedTensor contract implemented by Float8, MXFP8, and NVFP4 types, all resting on distributed and MoE infrastructure with a mirrored JAX API.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The Recipe family is the policy base at line 110, with DelayedScaling at 176, Float8CurrentScaling at 289, MXFP8BlockScaling at 345, and NVFP4BlockScaling at 502.
  • fp8_autocast at line 980 of a 2044-line module is the context manager that switches quantizers on when you enter a region.
  • TransformerEngineBaseModule at line 948 is the contract every fused module extends.
  • Linear at line 1904 of 1904-plus lines wraps its custom autograd function at 1807 for FP8 GEMMs.
  • LayerNormMLP at line 2156 fuses normalization with the gated MLP block so intermediate activations stay in low precision.
  • DotProductAttention at line 594 dispatches fused attention across supported backends.
  • QuantizedTensor defines the storage at line 54 and the Quantizer ABC at 371 that every format implements.
  • distributed.py is the 2271-line infrastructure file with activation recomputation at 241 and an RNG state tracker at 832.

Why You Need This

The first reason is that low precision is a moving target that no application wants to chase alone. In three years the field went from delayed-scaling FP8 on Hopper to per-tensor current scaling, to MXFP8 microscaling blocks, to NVFP4 four-bit training on Blackwell, with hybrid quantization and FP8 attention support arriving release by release. Each format has different scale layouts, kernel requirements, and numerics traps. TransformerEngine absorbs that churn behind one recipe interface, so moving your training from FP8 to MXFP8 is changing a constructor argument, not rewriting quantization logic across your model.

The second reason is integration depth with the frameworks you already use. The autocast API is deliberately shaped like torch.autocast, so adopting it is a wrapper around the forward pass rather than a restructure. Megatron-LM uses it for tensor, sequence, context, and expert parallelism with communication overlap; Accelerate and Lightning expose it as precision plugins; SageMaker’s model parallel library builds on the same primitives. Even better, the pytorch and jax packages share the recipe definitions in common, so a numerics decision made once applies to both ecosystems, and the JAX side ships its own dropless MoE path tuned for GB200-class systems. The attention package even carries inference plumbing, with a KVCacheManager at line 21 of attention/inference.py and a paged variant at 596, so the same library serves decode-time serving and training-time throughput.

The third reason is that the library treats fused kernels and quantization as one problem, not two. A naive FP8 implementation quantizes weights and activations, runs a fast GEMM, then pays the savings back in elementwise glue. The modules here fuse the glue into the kernels: LayerNormLinear folds the norm into the GEMM epilogue, LayerNormMLP keeps the entire norm-plus-expansion block in low precision, GroupedLinear batches expert weights into single calls, and the attention stack dispatches to fused backends including FP8 attention. CUDA graph support in a 1735-line graph.py then captures the steady state so launch overhead disappears at scale. Throughput comes from the whole chain, and the whole chain is here.

The detailed map: the recipe hierarchy and autocast region manager, the fused module family, the quantized tensor zoo, MoE routing and permutation, runtime infrastructure from CUDA graphs to fused optimizers, and the JAX mirror with debugging tools.

The recipe layer is the policy brain, and it is refreshingly small. Recipe at line 110 is a dataclass-style base, and the four public strategies are subclasses in the same file: DelayedScaling at 176 tracks amax history over a window and is the classic Hopper-era recipe; Float8CurrentScaling at 289 computes scales from the current step’s maximums; MXFP8BlockScaling at 345 and NVFP4BlockScaling at 502 encode Blackwell’s hardware microscaling formats. Policy objects carry no tensors; they are declarative. The mechanism lives in quantization.py, which opens by probing hardware support with functions like check_fp8_support at 191, then provides fp8_model_init at 886 so parameters are born ready for quantization, and fp8_autocast at 980, which on entry pushes the recipe’s quantizers into a global manager and on exit restores the previous state. The QuantizerRole and QuantizerRequest types at lines 59 and 117 make the handoff explicit.

The quantized tensor zoo is where formats become data. QuantizedTensorStorage at line 54 holds the raw bytes and scale planes, and the Quantizer ABC at 371 defines the quantize and dequantize contract. Each format then gets its own file: Float8Tensor at line 440 with its current-scaling quantizer at 197, Float8BlockwiseQTensor at 258 of the blockwise file, plus MXFP8 and NVFP4 siblings in their own modules, and a HybridTensor and GroupedTensor for mixed and batched cases. Two functions in quantized_tensor.py, prepare_for_saving at 291 and restore_from_saved at 318, manage the awkward autograd moment when quantized activations must be stashed for backward without defeating the memory savings that motivated them.

The fused modules are the biggest files in the package and the least negotiable to hand-write. TransformerEngineBaseModule at 948 centralizes weight initialization, quantization mode selection, and reset mechanics. Linear reaches line 1904 because its autograd function at 1807 must handle every combination of quantized and unquantized inputs, weight caching, and gradient accumulation in FP8. LayerNormLinear at 1546 and LayerNormMLP at 2156 push fusion further, and GroupedLinear at 1605 exists for MoE, where dozens of expert GEMMs must batch into few kernel launches. On top sit DotProductAttention at 594, a torch-compatible MultiheadAttention at 48 of multi_head_attention.py, and the TransformerLayer at line 71 that assembles the canonical block with DropPath at 46.

The MoE and infrastructure layers round out the system. Token routing lives in a 561-line router.py, expert placement and collectives in a 1245-line ep.py, and the token sort-and-unsort dance in permutation.py’s 1347 lines, all exposed through an operation graph whose dispatch and combine operations sit in the 38-file ops package. Around everything, distributed.py provides activation recomputation at 241 and deterministic RNG tracking at 832, cpu_offload.py moves state to host memory across 944 lines with a 751-line v1 variant kept for compatibility, and the fused optimizers package ships fused Adam, SGD, and multi-tensor apply. The JAX mirror keeps the same recipe objects and adds its own fp8_autocast at line 814 of jax/quantize/helper.py. A 21-file debug package, wired through debug/init.py, rounds it out with buffers and hooks for inspecting exactly what the quantizers did to your tensors, which is the difference between guessing at a loss spike and reading it.

From Install to FP8 Training

The package builds from source against your CUDA toolchain, so the README recommends no-build-isolation and prebuilt NGC containers:

pip install --no-build-isolation "transformer_engine[pytorch]"
# or, in a ready environment:
docker run --gpus all -it --rm nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:YY.MM-py3

The canonical usage is a context manager around the forward pass, straight from the project’s getting-started flow:

import torch
import transformer_engine.pytorch as te
from transformer_engine.common.recipe import DelayedScaling

linear = te.Linear(768, 3072, bias=True)

recipe = DelayedScaling()
with te.fp8_autocast(enabled=True, fp8_recipe=recipe):
    out = linear(torch.randn(16, 128, 768, device="cuda"))

Inside the context, the Linear’s weights and the input quantize through the active recipe, the GEMM runs on FP8 tensor cores, and scales update automatically. Swap DelayedScaling for Float8CurrentScaling, MXFP8BlockScaling, or NVFP4BlockScaling and the same two lines address three generations of hardware formats.

Honest limits: the hardware floor is real. FP8 needs Hopper or newer, MXFP8 and NVFP4 need Blackwell, and on Ampere you get FP16 and BF16 optimizations only, so the library is exactly as universal as NVIDIA’s product line. Building from source ties you to specific CUDA, cuDNN, and PyTorch version combinations, which is why the NGC container is the advertised path rather than a convenience. The JAX API, while sharing recipes, is a separate surface with its own maturity curve. Debugging low-precision numerics stays genuinely hard; the debug package helps, but scale-factor bugs still look like mysterious loss spikes. And the abstraction rewards standard architectures: highly custom blocks may fall back to unquantized paths silently. None of this dims the achievement, which is making an eight-bit world navigable with a context manager, and doing it for both of the frameworks that matter.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of NVIDIA/TransformerEngine: how recipes, an autocast region manager, a family of quantized tensors, fused modules from Linear to TransformerLayer, and expert-parallel MoE machinery put FP8, MXFP8, and NVFP4 training behind a one-line context manager for PyTorch and JAX.
